# Discussion

In this prospective, multicentre observational study,
we recaptured `r round(recovery_pct_final, 1)`% of the sevoflurane
with `r n_agcs["final"]` CONTRAfluran canisters
across `r n_center["final"]` hospitals in two European countries.
This represents `r round(zeosys_sevo_weight_kg, 1)` kg of recovered sevoflurane
from a total of `r round(sevo_final_kg, 1)` kg used
in our study cohort of `r n_cases_inhalational` inhalational anaesthesia cases.

These findings are considerably lower than the 34% capture efficiency
reported in a previous single-centre study for CONTRAfluran and sevoflurane [@Gibb2025].

Of the `r n_eligible` eligible canisters we selected `r n_agcs["final"]` for the desorption process by
nearest-neighbour clustering to generate a representative sample and avoid the
selection of extreme cases.
For example, two of the `r n_excl_outlier` excluded canisters showed unexpectedly low weight gain
despite receiving the full allocation of `r n_bottles_per_or` sevoflurane bottles.
In one OR, a large proportion of procedures used the Da Vinci surgical robot,
which may have limited sevoflurane exposure due to high gas exchange in the
capnoperitoneum.
In the other, extended TIVA phases may have allowed
previously adsorbed sevoflurane to desorb from the activated carbon
[@Kalmar2024c; @Wenzel2024].
Retrospective review further revealed that the SENSOfluran indicator unit
in this OR had not been recalibrated within the manufacturer's recommended
service interval during the study period,
potentially rendering canister exchange timing unreliable.
Both cases illustrate that absolute canister loading depends not only
on the total amount of sevoflurane administered
but also on the temporal distribution and proportion of inhalational anaesthesia.
This limits direct comparisons of capture efficiency across ORs.
Automatic bypass systems that disconnect the canister during TIVA phases
could reduce desorption losses and should be evaluated.
However, if we had included these canisters, the capture efficiency would have been even
lower.

In the LASSO regression and the corresponding stability selection
with `r length(clustering_columns)` candidate predictors,
the median fresh gas flow during inhalational anaesthesia
in intubated patients undergoing non-laparoscopic surgery
was the only stable predictor of higher canister *in vivo* mass transfer.

The fresh gas flow is a proxy for total sevoflurane exposure
and has previously been identified as a major determinant of exposure [@Shelton2022;@Gandhi2024;@Gibb2024b;@Gibb2025].
Consequently, a higher fresh gas flow is associated with higher capture efficiency,
as a greater proportion of the anaesthetic is wasted and enters the canister.

In our data, the use of a water trap between the anaesthesia machine and the
CONTRAfluran canister
was associated with higher recapture in the LASSO regression.
The water trap may have a protective effect against moisture accumulation in the activated carbon.
Coconut shell activated carbon shows a sharp decline in adsorption capacity
once water uptake exceeds approximately 30% of the sorbent mass [@Abiko2010].
In our canisters,
approximately `r round((1 - zeosys_yield) * 100, 0)`% of the weight gain was water rather than sevoflurane.
This suggests that moisture accumulation may have reduced the adsorption capacity.

The canisters were weighed twice at ZeoSys before desorption.
During these `r zeosys_storage_days` days
the `r n_agcs["final"]` canisters lost `r round(zeosys_total_wloss_g, 0)` g of weight.
This corresponds to almost two thirds of a sevoflurane bottle.
The additional desorption during transport and storage
before the first ZeoSys weighing was not quantified.
The true loss is therefore even higher.
This spontaneous desorption during storage was described in a previous study [@Gibb2025].
It highlights the need for short storage times and fast processing.

## Limitations

The study protocol originally specified at least four batches of 20 canisters,
but operational constraints at ZeoSys required batches of 80 canisters.
This protocol deviation precludes between-batch comparisons of desorption yield
and limits the primary outcome to a single-point estimate
without an empirical measure of batch-to-batch variability.
The sample size was determined by this operational minimum
and not by a formal power calculation.
The study may therefore be underpowered
to detect clinically meaningful differences in capture efficiency.

Given the ratio of `r length(clustering_columns)` candidate predictors to `r n_agcs["final"]` observations,
this analysis was exploratory and hypothesis-generating.

A further source of uncertainty concerns the `r n_excl_lost` canisters
that could not be located at ZeoSys before desorption.
It is unclear whether these were lost during postal transit,
received but not matched to the study inventory,
or misplaced at some other point in the collection chain.
For one third of them
the courier's delivery receipt confirms arrival at ZeoSys.

The fresh gas flow is the main predictor identified by our exploratory analysis.
Due to the pragmatic approach, it
was recorded as a single reading 15 minutes after induction,
not as a continuous average over the case.
Intraoperative flow adjustments are common in clinical practice,
so the recorded value may not accurately represent the true exposure.

Since individual saturation levels were not assessed,
the relative contribution of incomplete canister loading
to the reported capture efficiency cannot be quantified.

Finally, participation was voluntary,
and the centres that joined may not represent the wider anaesthesiology community.
Institutions committed to environmental sustainability tend to use low-flow anaesthesia,
which would be associated with a lower capture efficiency.
Although the study was conducted in two countries,
Germany and Austria share similar healthcare systems,
anaesthesia training, and clinical practice,
which limits the generalisability of the findings.
